953.title: Moroccan scholarship
953.hook: Fez and Marrakesh as cities of scholars, Sufis and craftsmen
953.howItsDone: In Fez and Marrakesh, historic madrasahs, mosques and saints' tombs are still visited, students still study at al-Qarawiyyin, and crafts such as zellij tilework are still practiced and taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tawhid, the oneness of God, which named the Almohads, the movement that replaced the Almoravids. Your line was: renewal from the desert.

Tap, tap, tap. In a workshop in Fez, a craftsman holds a small hammer and a square of glazed tile, and chips it into a tiny shape, a star point, a curved petal. Piece after piece will be laid face down, fitted together like a puzzle and set in plaster, until they become a wall that glitters. Across the lane, in the courtyard of a college, students sit reading among tiles cut by hands like his. In the old cities of Morocco, the scholar and the craftsman worked within a few steps of each other.
screen: `TAP, TAP — A TILE IS CUT.` → `A PUZZLE BECOMES A WALL.` → `THE SCHOLAR AND THE CRAFTSMAN.`

segments.voice: In Fez, the city's learning gathered around the mosque of al-Qarawiyyin, founded, as the chronicle you heard last week tells it, by Fatimah al-Fihri. Around it, rulers and donors added madrasahs: courtyards with a fountain, rooms for students upstairs, a prayer hall, walls of carved cedar, carved plaster and tilework. Marrakesh, founded by the Almoravids, became another city of learning in the south, with its own mosques, colleges and markets. In both, learning wasn't shut away. It lived next to the tanneries, the copper beaters and the book binders. Marrakesh also honors a group that tradition calls its seven saints, and the list joins two kinds of learning. One is Qadi Iyad, a judge and a scholar of hadith and law. Another is al-Jazuli, a Sufi whose book of blessings on the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is still recited. A judge and a mystic, side by side, honored by the same city. And the craftsmen? A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, number 2072, says nobody has eaten better food than what they earn by the work of their own hands, and that the prophet David ate from the work of his hands. Work with the hands wasn't a step down from study; it was honored too. So Moroccan scholarship is wider than a man with a book: the book, the student's room, the cut tile on the wall, the saint's tomb at the end of the lane. Cities of learning.
screen: `FEZ AROUND THE QARAWIYYIN.` · `MADRASAHS OF CEDAR, PLASTER, TILE.` · `A JUDGE AND A MYSTIC, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE WORK OF YOUR OWN HANDS.` · then, large: `CITIES OF LEARNING.`

segments.voice: Here's a craft word from Morocco: zellij, the cut glazed tilework from the hook; say it quietly. Then look at your own hands and think of one thing they know how to make or mend, bread, a shelf, a stitch, a careful page of handwriting, and hold that skill in mind the way a scholar holds a text. If you pray, give thanks for the work of your hands; if you don't, simply notice what they can do.

954.title: The Maghreb's Maliki school
954.hook: the Maliki school of law becomes the tradition of North and West Africa
954.carry: the school of medina traveled west
954.howItsDone: The Maliki school is followed in North and West Africa, the Muwatta of Imam Malik is still studied, and some Maliki worshippers pray with their arms at their sides.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Moroccan scholarship, Fez and Marrakesh, where scholars, Sufis and craftsmen shared the same lanes. Your line was: cities of learning.

A caliph admires a book, a collection of hadith and legal rulings by a scholar in Medina. He makes an offer: let this be the law for every land, copied out and sent to every city, so everyone follows one book. The scholar says no. The companions of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, he answers, scattered to many lands, and the people there learned from them. Let them keep what they have. That's how tradition tells it, and the scholar was Malik ibn Anas. His book stayed one voice among several, and yet it traveled further west than he ever did.
screen: `ONE BOOK FOR EVERY LAND?` → `THE SCHOLAR SAYS NO.` → `HIS BOOK TRAVELS WEST ANYWAY.`

segments.voice: Malik lived and taught in Medina, the Prophet's own city. His book is the Muwatta, a title that can be rendered the well-trodden path, the way already smoothed by feet. What made his method his own: alongside the Qur'an and the hadith, he gave great weight to the practice of the people of Medina, what the community there actually did, handed down from the generation that had lived beside the Prophet. If Medina still did it, that counted as evidence. Students heard the Muwatta from Malik and carried it home. Some went west. In Kairouan, in what is now Tunisia, scholars gathered his teaching into great law books. In al-Andalus, a student's copy of the Muwatta became the version people learned. From there the school spread through the Maghreb, and along the trade routes across the Sahara into West Africa. Yesterday's Qadi Iyad was a Maliki judge; the Almoravids held to Maliki law closely. One visible sign: some Malikis pray with their arms at their sides rather than folded. A Maliki is not a different kind of Muslim. The schools of Sunni law, the Hanafi, the Maliki, the Shafi'i and the Hanbali, share the same Qur'an and prayers, and differ in method and detail. Sunni scholars have long treated the four as ways of reading the same sources, not rival faiths. Shia Muslims have their own schools of law, such as the Ja'fari. That closes this stretch on Cairo, the Maghreb and the scholars. The school of Medina traveled west.
screen: `MALIK OF MEDINA.` · `THE MUWATTA — THE WELL-TRODDEN PATH.` · `KAIROUAN, AL-ANDALUS, WEST AFRICA.` · `SCHOOLS DIFFER IN METHOD, NOT FAITH.` · then, large: `THE SCHOOL OF MEDINA TRAVELED WEST.`

segments.voice: Think of the mosque nearest you, a Muslim friend or neighbor, or the country your family comes from: do you know which school of law they follow? Then bring to mind Malik's answer to the caliph, let the people keep what they learned. If you pray, ask for respect for those who pray a little differently; if you don't, hold that picture of one path walked in many ways.
Muwatta. Malik of Medina's book of law, the well-trodden path, whose school traveled west and took root in North and West Africa. Today's word.
Your line: the school of medina traveled west. Different methods, the same Qur'an. Day nine hundred fifty-four, done.

955.title: Jerusalem, 1099
955.hook: the First Crusade takes Jerusalem with great slaughter
955.howItsDone: Muslims say "inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un" (we are God's, and to Him we return) at news of a death or loss, and al-Aqsa in Jerusalem is honored as the place of the Night Journey.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Muwatta, Malik's book, and the Maliki school his students carried west from Medina. Your line was: the school of medina traveled west.

A group of refugees reaches Baghdad in the month of Ramadan. They have come a long way, from Syria and from Jerusalem. A judge brings them into the caliph's court, and they tell what they saw. The chronicler Ibn al-Athir says their story brought tears to the eyes of those who heard it. Then he adds a line about the rulers: they were divided among themselves, and nothing was done. This part of the path turns to the Crusades, the Mongols and the Mamluks, and it starts with the city those refugees had fled: Jerusalem.
screen: `REFUGEES REACH BAGHDAD.` → `THE COURT WEEPS.` → `THE RULERS ARE DIVIDED.`

segments.voice: Jerusalem matters in Islam because of a journey. The Qur'an opens one of its surahs with it. In Pickthall's translation: "Glorified be He Who carried His servant by night from the Inviolable Place of Worship to the Far Distant Place of Worship the neighbourhood whereof We have blessed." Muslims understand the Far Distant Place of Worship, al-Masjid al-Aqsa, to be in Jerusalem, and tradition says believers once faced toward it in prayer, before the Ka'bah. So it was holy ground, shared in different ways with Jews and Christians, who hold it holy too. Armies from western Europe, the Franks of the First Crusade, marched a long way to take it. When the city fell, they killed a great many of the people inside. Muslim chroniclers like Ibn al-Athir describe killing in the Aqsa mosque itself, among scholars and devout people who had come to live near it. A chronicler of Damascus, Ibn al-Qalanisi, writes that Jews were burned in their synagogue. Chroniclers among the Franks recorded the killing too. Nobody's numbers can be trusted, so i won't give any. The Qur'an gives words for a moment of loss like this. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." Those words are still said at news of a loss. Jerusalem, for a long time after, was a city in grief. And the refugees in Baghdad had named the problem the next generations would have to answer: a divided people.
screen: `THE NIGHT JOURNEY TO AL-AQSA.` · `HOLY GROUND, SHARED IN MANY WAYS.` · `THE CITY FALLS, THE KILLING BEGINS.` · `WE ARE ALLAH'S, AND UNTO HIM RETURNING.` · then, large: `A CITY IN GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the city that day, Muslims in the mosque, Jews in their synagogue, people of every faith in the streets, soldiers on every side; you don't need faces or numbers, just hold them all as people. If you pray, you can pray for all who died there with the words the Qur'an gives for loss: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, we are God's, and to Him we return. If you don't pray, simply keep a silence for them.
Jerusalem. The city of the Night Journey and the Aqsa mosque, holy to Muslims, Jews and Christians, and the city taken with great slaughter in the First Crusade. Today's word.
Your line: a city in grief. Behind every count were people with names. See you tomorrow.

956.title: Salah al-Din
956.hook: the Kurdish sultan who united Egypt and Syria
956.howItsDone: Salah al-Din's tomb in Damascus is still visited, and Ibn Shaddad's biography of him is still read.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jerusalem, taken in the First Crusade, and refugees in Baghdad telling their story to rulers too divided to answer. Your line was: a city in grief.

As if he were being driven to his death. That, in one account, is how a young officer later described riding with his uncle's army to Egypt. He hadn't wanted to go. His name was Yusuf, son of Ayyub, from a Kurdish family that served the Turkish ruler of Syria, Nur al-Din. He would become known by an honorific, a title of praise: Salah al-Din, the righteousness of the faith. Some in the west learned to call him Saladin. The reluctant officer would spend his life on yesterday's problem: a divided people.
screen: `A RELUCTANT YOUNG OFFICER.` → `YUSUF, SON OF AYYUB.` → `THE RIGHTEOUSNESS OF THE FAITH.`

segments.voice: In Egypt, the Fatimid caliphs still ruled from Cairo, the city you met earlier this month. Salah al-Din's uncle became their vizier and soon died, and the post passed to the young Yusuf. Then he did something quiet and enormous: he had the Friday sermon in Egypt said in the name of the Sunni caliph, the Abbasid in Baghdad, not the Fatimid one. The Fatimid line came to an end. When Nur al-Din died, Salah al-Din moved into Syria and, over years of bargaining and battle, brought Damascus, Aleppo and other cities under his rule. Now Egypt and Syria answered to one ruler. Not everyone welcomed him. Some of Nur al-Din's family and followers saw a servant taking his master's lands, and said so. His biographer, the judge Ibn Shaddad, who served beside him, paints a man who prayed, listened to hadith read aloud, wept easily, and gave away so much that he left almost nothing at his death. Biographers can love their subjects, so it's fair to hold that portrait a little loosely. Whatever else drove him, the work of his life, as these sources tell it, was bringing divided lands under one rule. The Qur'an has a line for that hope. In Pickthall's translation: "And hold fast, all of you together, to the cable of Allah, and do not separate." A Kurdish officer, serving a Turkish lord, uniting Arab lands. The kurdish sultan.
screen: `THE FATIMID CALIPHATE ENDS.` · `EGYPT AND SYRIA UNDER ONE RULER.` · `IBN SHADDAD'S PORTRAIT.` · `HOLD FAST, ALL OF YOU TOGETHER.` · then, large: `THE KURDISH SULTAN.`

957.title: Jerusalem, 1187
957.hook: Salah al-Din retakes Jerusalem and lets many ransom out or leave in peace
957.howItsDone: Muslims retell Salah al-Din's taking of Jerusalem in sermons, books and classrooms, and the release of people who could not pay the ransom is often told as an example of mercy in victory.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Salah al-Din, the Kurdish officer who brought Egypt and Syria under one rule. Your line was the kurdish sultan.

The city has surrendered. Inside the walls, families are counting coins on kitchen tables. The terms, as the sultan's own secretary records them, are plain: each person may pay a ransom, take their goods and walk out of the gate within a set time. Some can pay. Some can't, and they know it. At the gate, the clerks sit with their lists, and everyone waits to see what the winner will do about the people with nothing to hand over. The winner is Salah al-Din, and the city is the one Arabic calls the holy. Today: Jerusalem.
screen: `THE CITY SURRENDERS.` → `A RANSOM TO WALK OUT.` → `WHAT ABOUT THOSE WHO CAN'T PAY?`

segments.voice: In Arabic, Jerusalem is usually al-Quds, the holy. It's the city of the Aqsa mosque, linked with the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his night journey, and the hadith collections report that the believers once faced toward it in prayer, before the qiblah turned to Mecca. The Crusaders had held it, and Muslim chroniclers remembered the day they took it as a day of killing. So payback might have been expected. What the accounts describe instead is a surrender on terms. Imad al-Din, the sultan's secretary, who was there, writes of the ransom and the gate. Then the part beyond the terms. The sultan's brother, al-Adil, the accounts say, asked for a group of the poor as a gift, and set them free. Salah al-Din released others himself, among them the old, and let widows go. They also say that those who could not pay and were not freed were taken captive. Mercy came, and it didn't reach everyone. It was a choice made at a gate, by people, imperfectly. The story sits close to a teaching in the Qur'an. In surah an-Nahl, if the believers punish, the punishment must match the wrong done to them, no more; and if they bear it patiently, that is better. Surah ash-Shura makes the same turn: an injury may be answered with its like, but whoever pardons and makes peace, their reward is with Allah. The Qur'an allows a fair answer. It praises the pardon. Winning is when that costs most, because winning is when you could.
screen: `AL-QUDS — THE HOLY.` · `A RANSOM AT THE GATE.` · `THOSE WHO COULD NOT PAY.` · `PARDON IS BETTER, THE QUR'AN SAYS.` · then, large: `MERCY IN VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind somewhere you're ahead right now: an argument you won, a sibling who owes you an apology. Notice the pull to press it, then choose one small mercy, like letting the point drop or leaving the final message unsent. If you pray, ask Allah for a soft heart in the moment you could be hard; if not, hold that person in mind with some kindness.

Your line: mercy in victory. A fair answer is allowed; the pardon is praised. That's plenty for today.

958.title: The Mongols
958.hook: armies from the steppe sweep through Central Asia and Persia
958.howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un, from surah al-Baqarah, when they hear of a death or any loss, and Friday sermons sometimes close with supplications for people suffering war.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jerusalem, a ransom at the gate, and some who couldn't pay set free. Your line was mercy in victory.

A caravan of merchants rides into a border town called Otrar, on the eastern edge of the lands of the Khwarazm-shah. They've come from the ruler of the steppe peoples, to trade. As the chroniclers tell it, the town's governor accuses them of being spies and has them killed. An envoy comes to complain, and he is killed too. A quarrel over goods and pride on a frontier, the kind of thing a governor might expect to forget. It was not forgotten. Today: the Mongols.
screen: `MERCHANTS RIDE INTO OTRAR.` → `KILLED AS SPIES.` → `IT WAS NOT FORGOTTEN.`

segments.voice: The Mongols were peoples of the steppe, the wide grasslands north of China, horsemen brought under one ruler, Chinggis Khan. After Otrar, their armies came west, through Bukhara and Samarkand, cities of mosques, markets and scholars, and on into Persia. The chronicles describe cities that resisted and were emptied, and cities that opened their gates and were spared. They are hard reading. The historian Ibn al-Athir was writing a great history of the world in Mosul when the news arrived. He writes that he held back from writing this part for a long while, because he could not bear to. When he did, he said he wished he had died before it happened and been forgotten, words that echo Mary's cry in surah Maryam. A historian whose job was to write everything down, wishing he hadn't lived to write this. That's today's line: the storm from the east. It's a picture, not a weather report: how it felt to people who had no way to stop it. So what does a believer say when the news is that bad? You met the words at Jerusalem's fall; here is where they come from. Surah al-Baqarah describes those who, when misfortune strikes, say, in Pickthall's English: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." In Arabic: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Muslims say it at a death, and at any loss or bad news, large or small. It doesn't explain the storm, or pretend it isn't happening. It simply says who the grieving belong to while it passes over.
screen: `RIDERS FROM THE STEPPE.` · `BUKHARA, SAMARKAND, PERSIA.` · `A HISTORIAN WHO COULDN'T WRITE IT.` · `WE ARE ALLAH'S, AND TO HIM WE RETURN.` · then, large: `THE STORM FROM THE EAST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a place where people are living through war right now, and let one person there become clear: a grandmother who can't leave, a child who knows the sound of planes, a doctor who hasn't slept. If you pray, ask Allah for their safety and for help to reach them; if you don't, simply keep them in mind, and don't look away early.
The Mongols. Horsemen of the steppe, united under Chinggis Khan, whose armies swept through Central Asia and Persia. Today's word.
Your line: the storm from the east. Next, the storm reaches Baghdad. See you tomorrow.

959.title: Baghdad, 1258
959.hook: Baghdad falls, the caliph is killed, and chronicles say the Tigris ran dark with ink from books
959.howItsDone: Muslims treat copies of the Qur'an with care, keeping them clean and high, and the fall of Baghdad is remembered in histories and classrooms as a loss of lives and of learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Mongols, riders from the steppe, and a historian who could barely bring himself to write it. Your line was the storm from the east.

What color is a river after a library has been thrown into it? Later chroniclers had an answer, and people still repeat it. The Tigris, they wrote, ran dark with the ink of books washed off their pages. Whether it happened exactly that way, historians argue. But nobody had to invent the grief behind it. The storm from the east had reached the city of the caliphs, a city of mosques, markets, hospitals and libraries on that river. Today: Baghdad.
screen: `WHAT COLOR IS THE RIVER?` → `DARK WITH INK, THEY WROTE.` → `THE CITY OF THE CALIPHS.`

segments.voice: Baghdad was the capital of the Abbasid caliphs, the city of the House of Wisdom, where scholars gathered and books were copied and translated. Hulagu, a grandson of Chinggis Khan, led the Mongol armies toward it. The city was besieged, and the walls were breached. The chronicles say the caliph, al-Musta'sim, went out to the Mongol camp to surrender, hoping to save his people. The city was sacked anyway, and the caliph was killed. The accounts differ on how he died, and on almost every number, so the numbers stay where they are, in dispute. Then the river of ink. Notice what people chose to remember. Not only the dead, though they mourned the dead. The books. Why would that picture last? Because of where Islam begins. The first words revealed to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in surah al-'Alaq, are a command to read, and they say of Allah, in Pickthall's English: "Who teacheth by the pen." A whole civilization had grown around that pen: the Qur'an copied by hand, hadith written down, law, poetry, medicine, maps. Losing the books could feel like having the pen knocked out of your hand. And yet the story didn't end there. Copies existed in other cities. Scholars carried what they knew in memory. People who could write kept writing. The river of ink is a picture of loss, and of what a people treasured, because you only grieve like that for something you loved.
screen: `THE CITY OF THE HOUSE OF WISDOM.` · `THE CALIPH GOES OUT, AND IS KILLED.` · `THEY REMEMBERED THE BOOKS.` · `WHO TEACHETH BY THE PEN.` · then, large: `THE RIVER OF INK.`

segments.voice: If you can, pick up a book now: a Qur'an, a family Bible, a grandmother's recipe notebook, a school book with someone's name inside the cover. Feel its weight, and think of who wrote it, who copied or printed it, who kept it until it reached you, then give it one small act of care, like wiping off the dust. If you pray, thank Allah for the pen and those who carried it; if not, simply hold the book a moment longer before you set it down.
Baghdad. The city of the Abbasid caliphs on the Tigris, sacked by Hulagu's army, its caliph killed, and its books, the chronicles say, thrown in the river. Today's word.
Your line: the river of ink. The pen was knocked loose, not lost. Day nine hundred fifty-nine, done.

chat.says: Why do people remember Baghdad's fall by its books, and not only its dead?
